Chapter 12: Sayings from the journey

Acharn Sujin did not give long lectures on the journey. She asked questions and said short things, and Nina wrote them down. Here are twelve of her sayings, with the place where each was said. They make a short way back through the book.

“When we “follow the stream” we can understand that all events are only conditioned dhammas.”

1. “The Abhidhamma is not in the book”. Said about the Abhidhamma (the higher teaching), the part of the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets) that describes every reality1. The description is in the book. The realities themselves, seeing, hearing, feeling, liking and disliking, are happening now, and that is where they have to be understood.

2. “Without patience one cannot attain enlightenment”. Said about the verses of the Dhammapada (the Buddha’s verses on the teaching) and the Ovāda Pāṭimokkha (the Exhortation2 to the Pāṭimokkha), where patience is named first. Nina writes: “We need great patience to develop understanding of all realities of our daily life.”

3. “Do you like it to be tired?” Asked of Alan at the tombs of the kings. He did not like it, “and then it became clear that he had aversion3.” The question works for hunger, a broken shower and a lost suitcase too. It shows the dosa (aversion) behind the tiredness.

4. “What is the use of being impatient?” Said to Nina after the night when the luggage was lost. “Only right understanding can see that it is useless.” Impatience does not bring the suitcase any faster.

5. “Where is that being? It is only a story in your mind.” Said about thinking of people. What is seen is colour; the person is thought of afterwards. “One can be alone at the moment of hearing sound, because there is no idea of anyone at that moment.”

6. “Now you are preparing.” Said when Nina asked how to prepare for the death of someone dear. “We can only prepare ourselves for a great loss by understanding the present moment more clearly.”

7. “It is just this moment.” Said when Nina asked Acharn Sujin whether she was tired, because she was yawning. Tiredness, like everything else, is one conditioned4 reality appearing now.

8. “Why do you want it? Develop it.” Said to Alan when he asked why understanding does not arise5 often. Wanting sati (awareness6) is lobha (attachment7), and the idea of “somebody with sati” is the self in the way. “There is no self who could plan to have sati.”

9. “When there are conditions for awareness, you can’t prevent it from arising”. Said to show that sati (awareness) is anattā (non-self8). Nina writes: “When the conditions9 are right it must arise and we do not have to do anything to cause its arising.”

10. “Instead of wanting to develop satipaṭṭhāna, one should develop kusala, being considerate for others.” Said about people who want satipaṭṭhāna (direct awareness of realities) and forget everything else. “Kindness, considerateness10, patience, all wholesome11 cetasikas are conditions for the arising of different levels of sati and pañña.”

11. “I always follow the stream”. Said in Istanbul, when Nina worried that a show would end late. “When we “follow the stream” we can understand that all events are only conditioned dhammas.”

12. “Develop it now, be aware now”. Nina writes that Acharn “often said” this, to people who thought that they could not attain enlightenment12 in this life and were ready to give up. “The understanding of this moment leads to the goal.”

What Nina took home. At the end of her introduction Nina thanks her teacher: “I am most grateful to Acharn for pointing out to us time and again that we should understand our life at this very moment. What she explained is completely in conformity with the Buddha’s teachings.” And at the end of her account of the journey: “There are opportunities for the development of right understanding in any situation and this conditions more patience. Our journey with Dhamma was most beneficial13.”

The pyramids are still standing in Egypt, and the Bosporus still runs through Istanbul. The travellers’ seeing of them lasted a moment each time and fell away. What they kept was something Nina says is “never lost”: the moments of listening, considering and understanding, “accumulated14 from one moment to the next moment so that they can arise again, later on.”

Where it comes from

This book follows A Journey with Dhamma in Egypt and Turkey by Nina van Gorkom, published by Zolag (www.zolag.co.uk) under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivs licence: the book “may be freely copied and distributed, but its contents must not be changed.” Nina’s book has an introduction and six chapters: Patience; Understanding the Present Moment; Clinging to Mindfulness; Conversations on Buddhism; An Interview on Buddhism; and Further Interviews between Gabi, Alan and Nina in Egypt. Chapters 1 and 2 of this book follow her introduction; Chapters 3 and 4 her first chapter; Chapters 5 and 6 her second; Chapters 7 and 8 her third; Chapter 9 her fourth; Chapters 10 and 11 her fifth and sixth.

Chapter 12 gathers sayings from the whole book.

Where this book quotes a sentence in quotation marks, the words are Nina’s, or the words of Acharn Sujin, Gabi, Alan or Ms Tuna as Nina wrote them down, or the words of the ancient texts in the translations she uses. Nothing in quotation marks has been changed, with one exception: in the book’s quotation of Dhammapada (the Buddha’s verses on the teaching) verse 315 the word “without” is misprinted as “wihout”, and this book prints it correctly. The book’s spelling of Pāḷi words is kept inside quotations (for example “bhavanga”, “Vipaakacittas”); outside quotations this book uses the usual spelling with the marks on the letters.

The ancient texts quoted in Nina’s book, and so in this one, are:

The Dhammapada (the Buddha’s verses on the teaching), verses 183, 184 and 315. The Ovāda Pāṭimokkha (the Exhortation to the Pāṭimokkha), the verses in which the Buddhas of the past gave the heart of their teaching to the monks, where patience is named first. The Itivuttaka (As It Was Said), The Twos, Chapter II, § 2, on looking at akusala (unwholesome) as akusala (unwholesome). The Visuddhimagga (the Path of Purity) by Buddhaghosa, Chapter IX, on loving-kindness, the danger of dosa (aversion) and the benefit of patience; and the question of the order of sīla (morality), samādhi (concentration) and paññā (understanding). The Harita Jātaka (the birth story of Harita), number 431, on truthfulness. The story of Visākhā, the lay disciple foremost in ministering to the Saṅgha (the order), told in the commentaries.

Where the ancient texts and modern scholars differ, this book follows the ancient texts, as Nina’s book does. Nothing has been added to the teaching that is not in her book. A few things have been left out as unsuited to young readers; in the Harita Jātaka (the birth story of Harita), this book says only that the ascetic broke his good conduct.

Nina van Gorkom’s books, including this one, can be read free of charge on abhidhamma.org and at zolag.co.uk.
